clinicalPearls: Caused by pathogenic variants in MYH7, the gene encoding slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain, with autosomal dominant inheritance
Typically an early-onset distal myopathy, often beginning in childhood or adolescence, though onset can extend into adulthood
Weakness starts in the anterior compartment of the lower legs, producing foot drop and weakness of great-toe and ankle dorsiflexion, classically with a 'hanging big toe' sign
Finger extensor and neck flexor weakness commonly follow, while progression is slow and many patients remain ambulant for decades
Because MYH7 also causes cardiomyopathy, cardiac surveillance is prudent even though overt cardiac involvement in Laing myopathy is variable
Creatine kinase is normal or only mildly elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern
Muscle biopsy may show fibre-type disproportion, type 1 fibre predominance, and sometimes cores or hyaline bodies, but findings can be non-specific so genetic confirmation is important
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic distal weakness distribution combined with MYH7 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Laing distal myopathy is caused by dominant variants in MYH7, which encodes the slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain expressed in type 1 skeletal muscle fibres and cardiac muscle. Mutant myosin impairs the assembly and function of the thick filament of the sarcomere, disturbing contraction of predominantly slow-twitch fibres. This selectively affects muscles rich in type 1 fibres, accounting for the early anterior lower-leg and neck flexor involvement, and the shared gene explains the potential for associated cardiac disease.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other causes of distal neurogenic foot drop
Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy with foot extensor weakness
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase (usually normal or mildly raised)
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm a myopathic, non-neurogenic process
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry and immunohistochemistry
Muscle MRI to define the pattern of selective muscle involvement
Targeted MYH7 sequencing or a distal myopathy gene panel
Baseline and periodic cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography
redFlags: Symptoms or signs of cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia given the MYH7 association
Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Respiratory muscle involvement with reduced vital capacity
Prominent dysphagia or bulbar features atypical for Laing myopathy
reference.prognosis: Progression is typically slow, and most patients retain independent walking well into adulthood, though distal weakness gradually extends more proximally over decades; life expectancy is usually normal unless significant cardiac or respiratory involvement develops.
pitfalls: Mistaking the foot drop for a peripheral neuropathy and missing the myopathic cause
Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes a myopathy
Over-interpreting non-specific biopsy changes without genetic confirmation
Neglecting cardiac screening given the MYH7 gene's cardiac role
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
GeneReviews: MYH7-related distal myopathy (Laing distal myopathy)
management: Manage supportively as no disease-modifying therapy exists, focusing on preserving mobility and function
Provide physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, with occupational therapy and walking aids as needed
Undertake baseline and periodic cardiac surveillance with ECG and echocardiography because MYH7 also causes cardiomyopathy, treating any conduction disease or cardiomyopathy that emerges
Monitor respiratory function and treat ventilatory involvement as weakness progresses
Involve orthopaedics and podiatry for foot deformity and contractures
Coordinate care through a specialist neuromuscular clinic
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for autosomal dominant inheritance, including cardiac evaluation of at-risk relatives
